fetched_contents.text: Pediatric Appendicitis - StatPearls Continuing Education Activity Appendicitis is one of the most common surgical conditions in children and demands a high index of suspicion based on history and physical exam findings. While the classic presentation includes periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, many pediatric cases begin with nonspecific symptoms, especially in younger children, where anatomical variation may obscure the diagnosis. Because of this variability, appendicitis should remain a key consideration in the differential diagnosis of any child presenting with abdominal pain. This activity reviews typical and atypical presentations, outlines recommended evaluation strategies—including clinical scoring systems and imaging approaches—and highlights current medical and surgical management trends. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in the diagnostic evaluation and timely, collaborative management of appendicitis in children, emphasizing the importance of coordinated interprofessional care across emergency medicine, pediatrics, radiology, and surgery to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce complications, and ensure prompt intervention. Objectives: * Identify clinical features that warrant suspicion of appendicitis in children presenting with abdominal pain. * Assess appropriate evaluation strategies for children suspected of having appendicitis, including history, physical exam, laboratory studies, and imaging. * Determine current management strategies for pediatric appendicitis, including indications for operative and nonoperative approaches. * Collaborate with interprofessional team members to improve care coordination for timely diagnosis and treatment of pediatric appendicitis. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic. Introduction Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency in children and a leading cause of pediatric abdominal pain. This condition involves acute inflammation of the vermiform appendix and warrants prompt recognition and intervention. In any child presenting with acute abdominal pain and no history of appendectomy, appendicitis should remain high on the differential. Anatomically, the appendix most commonly arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum and may occupy variable positions, eg, retrocecal or pelvic, which can influence clinical presentation. These various presentations can result in underrecognition of pediatric appendicitis, particularly in younger children with nonspecific or atypical symptoms. Delayed diagnosis increases the risk of perforation, peritonitis, and other complications, making timely evaluation critical to improving outcomes.[1][2][3] Etiology Appendicitis most commonly results from obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, which may be caused by lymphoid hyperplasia, fecaliths, foreign bodies, or, less commonly, tumors.[4][5] The appendix contains abundant lymphoid tissue in the mucosa and submucosa, especially in children and adolescents, making it particularly susceptible to lymphoid hyperplasia. This immune response can narrow or occlude the lumen, leading to increased intraluminal pressure, bacterial overgrowth, ischemia, and subsequent inflammation of the appendiceal wall. Epidemiology Appendicitis is the most common surgical condition in children, with an annual incidence in the United States estimated at 83 cases per 100,000 population.[6] Although it can occur at any age, the peak incidence is between 15 and 19 years.[7] Appendicitis is slightly more common in males than females, with a male-to-female ratio of approximately 1.4:1. The lifetime risk is about 8.6% in males and 6.7% in females.[8] Globally, incidence rates vary based on geographic and socioeconomic factors, with higher rates observed in industrialized countries. Improved sanitation and dietary changes have been associated with declining incidence in some regions, while increasing rates are noted in others undergoing dietary Westernization. Children have a higher risk of perforation compared to adults, with perforation occurring in approximately 30% of pediatric hospital admissions for appendicitis.[9] This may be due to nonspecific presentations that mimic other gastrointestinal illnesses, contributing to delays in diagnosis and treatment.[10] Pathophysiology Appendicitis typically begins with luminal obstruction, which leads to continued mucus secretion, increased intraluminal pressure, and progressive distention of the appendix. As pressure builds, venous outflow is compromised, resulting in ischemia, bacterial overgrowth, and eventual necrosis.[11] If untreated, this process culminates in perforation and peritonitis.[12] Pain initially presents as poorly localized periumbilical discomfort due to visceral afferent fibers that follow sympathetic innervation and enter the spinal cord at T10. The pain localizes to the right lower quadrant as inflammation progresses and involves the parietal peritoneum. History and Physical Clinical History The classic presentation of appendicitis begins with vague, colicky periumbilical or epigastric pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant within 24 hours of symptom onset. Abdominal pain often precedes vomiting and may be accompanied by anorexia and fever. Dysuria or hematuria can occur due to the appendix’s proximity to the urinary tract. Anorexia is common, but not universally present. Diarrhea may also be present and can lead to misdiagnosis as gastroenteritis, particularly in younger children. Typical symptoms are often absent in the pediatric population, especially in children younger than 5. History may include nonspecific complaints eg, diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, low-grade fever, or irritability in these cases. Signs (eg, lethargy, fever, or diffuse tenderness) may be the only clues in infants and toddlers. Slater, MD, MBA, University of Chicago Medicine, Chicago, IL ABSTRACT Background: Appendicitis is an extremely common disease with a variety of medical and surgical treatment approaches. A multidisciplinary expert panel was convened to develop evidence-based recommendations to support clinicians and patients in decisions regarding the diagnosis and treatment of appendicitis. Methods: A systematic review was conducted from 2010 to 2022 to answer 8 key questions relating to the diagnosis of appendicitis, operative or nonoperative management, and specific technical and post-operative issues for appendectomy. The results of this systematic review were then presented to a panel of adult and pediatric surgeons. Evidence-based recommendations were formulated using the GRADE methodology by subject experts. Conclusions: These recommendations should provide guidance with regard to current controversies in appendicitis. Evidence-based recommendations were formulated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology by subject matter experts. GRADE is a transparent framework used in the development of clinical practice guidelines, using the highest-level evidence available. Expert opinion was utilized in cases of insufficient data for an evidence-based recommendation. Recommendations for future research were also proposed. Interpretation of strong and conditional recommendations All guideline recommendations were assigned either a “strong” or “conditional” recommendation. The words “the guideline panel recommends” are used for strong recommendations, and “the guideline panel suggests” for conditional recommendations, as per the GRADE approach. This uncertainty may be due to a lack of high-quality evidence or variability in how individual patients value the outcomes of interest. fetched_contents.text: Validation and Comparison of Pediatric Appendicitis Scores and Management Strategies (Project SPASMS): Protocol for a Prospective Multicenter Observational Study Abstract Background Abdominal pain is a common reason for children to attend the Emergency Department (ED) with acute appendicitis being the most common surgical cause. Various clinical prediction scores (CPSs) have been developed to assist in determining the risk of appendicitis; however, CPSs have been inadequately validated in children and haphazardly adopted in Australia and New Zealand (ANZ) EDs. Objective This study aims to compare and validate various CPSs for diagnosing pediatric appendicitis in children presenting to ANZ EDs. Methods This prospective multicenter observational study across 10 ANZ EDs is recruiting children 5-17 years presenting to participating EDs with acute right-sided or generalized abdominal pain lasting ≤7 days and clinician suspicion of appendicitis. CPSs will be calculated by the study team from clinician-recorded data and clinician gestalt recorded on a visual analog scale. Accuracy of CPSs will be assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and proportions correctly identified as either low-risk or high-risk based on the CPSs published cutoffs. The final diagnosis of appendicitis will be confirmed on histopathology, and the absence of appendicitis confirmed by telephone, email, or a combination of both to follow up for those discharged directly from ED. Results This study received funding in July 2023 and started enrolment in August 2023. As of October 2024, we have enrolled and completed follow-up on 1227 participants with an expected end date in mid-2025. Conclusions This study aims to determine the best-performing CPS for diagnosing pediatric appendicitis in ANZ EDs. Implementation of this CPS in ANZ EDs has the potential to reduce health care costs, rationalize the use of health care resources, and improve the management and outcomes of childhood appendicitis. Trial Registration Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12622001293752; https://tinyurl.com/242wwenx International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID) DERR1-10.2196/67941 Keywords: pediatric, emergency medicine, clinical prediction scores, appendicitis, abdominal pain Introduction Background Abdominal pain is a common reason for children to attend the emergency department (ED), with acute appendicitis being the most frequent cause requiring surgical intervention [1]. Many clinical prediction scores (CPSs) [2-31] have been developed and ED clinicians are encouraged to use CPSs to assist with determining the risk of appendicitis [32]. Most CPSs involve calculating a score based on combinations of clinical features and laboratory findings to classify patients into low-, intermediate-, or high-risk. The most frequently used CPSs in children are the Alvarado score [2], the Pediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS) [3], and the pediatric appendicitis risk calculator (pARC) [4], with each based on different sets of collected variables. Evidence-based triage framework for pediatric appendicitis

The most important initial exam elements for pediatric appendicitis are history and physical examination findings, particularly right lower quadrant tenderness and other signs of appendiceal inflammation. StatPearls emphasizes that appendicitis should remain a key consideration in the differential diagnosis of any child presenting with abdominal pain, and that evaluation strategies include clinical scoring systems and imaging approaches [N1-F1]. The same source notes that the classic presentation begins with vague, colicky periumbilical or epigastric pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, with accompanying symptoms such as vomiting, anorexia, fever, and abdominal pain that may be nonspecific in younger children [N1-F1]. Physical examination, therefore, is central to the diagnostic process because it helps identify right lower quadrant tenderness and other signs that raise suspicion [N1-F1].

Pediatric appendicitis scoring fits into triage as a tool for risk stratification, not as a definitive diagnostic test. The evidence shows that clinical prediction scores (CPSs) have been developed to assist in determining the risk of appendicitis, and that they are calculated based on combinations of clinical features and laboratory findings [N2-F3]. However, the same source also notes that CPSs have been inadequately validated in children and are often used haphazardly in some settings, so they should be interpreted carefully [N2-F3]. The pediatric appendicitis score (PAS) is one of the most frequently used CPSs in children, and the evidence emphasizes that it is intended to predict appendicitis likelihood in children aged 3 to 18 years [N2-R1][N2-R2]. The best-practice guidance from the AJR article states that once appendicitis is suspected, no single history, physical examination, laboratory finding, or score can eliminate the need for imaging studies [N3-F4]. Therefore, scoring systems should be used alongside clinical judgment and not as a substitute for imaging when suspicion remains.

Recommended imaging sequence is ultrasound-first, with MRI next when ultrasound is inconclusive. The SAGES guideline says ultrasound is a reasonable first-line study given its low cost and lack of radiation, while CT and MRI are the most definitive imaging modalities [N1-R2]. The AJR article explicitly endorses a stepwise imaging approach that begins with graded compression ultrasound and proceeds to CT or MRI in select cases [N3-F4]. The ACR narrative also says that MRI may be indicated in children with intermediate clinical risk for acute appendicitis [N3-R1]. The AJR article further notes that some institutions use MRI as a replacement for CT to avoid radiation risks, although MRI remains uncommon in routine pediatric appendicitis workups [N3-F4]. Taken together, the strongest evidence-based sequence is: ultrasound first, then MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive or if higher diagnostic certainty is needed [N1-R2][N3-F4][N3-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports a structured triage pathway: initial clinical suspicion based on history and physical examination, use of pediatric appendicitis scoring as part of risk stratification, and ultrasound-first imaging with MRI as the next step when the result is inconclusive or when intermediate risk persists [N1-F1][N2-F3][N3-F4].

Pediatric appendicitis scoring fits into triage as a tool for risk stratification, not as a definitive diagnostic test. However, the same source also notes that CPSs have been inadequately validated in children and are often used haphazardly in some settings, so they should be interpreted carefully [N2-F3]. The pediatric appendicitis score (PAS) is one of the most frequently used CPSs in children, and the evidence emphasizes that it is intended to predict appendicitis likelihood in children aged 3 to 18 years [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Once appendicitis is suspected, the AJR article notes that no single history, physical examination, laboratory finding, or score can eliminate the need for imaging studies [N3-F4]. Therefore, scoring systems should be used alongside clinical judgment and not as a substitute for imaging when suspicion remains.

Recommended imaging sequence is ultrasound first, then MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive. The SAGES guideline says ultrasound is a reasonable first-line study given its low cost and lack of radiation, while CT and MRI are the most definitive imaging modalities [N1-R2]. The AJR article explicitly endorses a stepwise imaging approach that begins with graded compression ultrasound and proceeds to CT or MRI in select cases [N3-F4]. The ACR narrative also says that MRI may be indicated in children with intermediate clinical risk for acute appendicitis [N3-R1]. The AJR article further notes that some institutions use MRI as a replacement for CT to avoid radiation risks, although MRI remains uncommon in routine pediatric appendicitis workups [N3-F4]. Taken together, the strongest evidence-based sequence is: ultrasound first, then MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive or if higher diagnostic certainty is needed [N1-R2][N3-F4][N3-R1].

## 2) Grammar and style review

The patient’s proposed message is already reasonably clear and concise, but it can be tightened for even greater professionalism and readability. The sentence structure is straightforward and well suited to a medical message, with a logical sequence of actions: initial exam, scoring, ultrasound, MRI, and surgery consultation. However, the phrase “we want to ensure we address potential appendicitis thoroughly” is somewhat vague and could be made more precise. It also introduces a passive tone that may weaken the message’s directness. A better approach would be to state the purpose more actively, such as “we want to ensure we thoroughly evaluate every potential case of appendicitis” [N4-R2][N4-R5].

Word choice is mostly professional, but a few improvements would strengthen clarity and tone. “Use” and “obtain” are both acceptable, but “calculate” is more precise than “use” when referring to a scoring system. “If suspicion remains high” is slightly less precise than “if suspicion remains” because “high” is not defined in the evidence provided here. “Strongly suggestive” is a good term for imaging findings, but it is already included in the patient’s draft, so there is little need to repeat it. The phrase “we want to ensure we address potential appendicitis thoroughly” is also redundant because “address” and “thoroughly” overlap in meaning. A more concise and professional alternative would be “we want to ensure we thoroughly evaluate every potential case of appendicitis” [N5-R3][N5-R5].

There is minimal ambiguity in the proposed message, but one area of possible confusion is whether the scoring system is being used as a diagnostic tool or merely as a risk-stratification tool. Because the evidence supports scoring as part of risk stratification rather than as a standalone diagnostic test [N2-F3][N3-F4], the wording should reflect that nuance. The draft is already close to the right balance, but it could be strengthened by making the role of scoring more explicit.

## 3) Professional tone revision

The patient’s concern about the tone is valid: the original phrase “everyone must do their best to avoid mistakes” can sound negative or blaming. A better professional phrasing is to focus on thorough evaluation and shared responsibility rather than on individual error. The evidence supports this approach because it emphasizes that careful assessment and teamwork are essential for minimizing error and improving outcomes [N4-R2][N4-R5]. A safer and more professional phrasing is “we want to ensure we thoroughly evaluate every potential case of appendicitis,” which focuses on the evaluation process rather than blaming individuals [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Another positive alternative is “we want to ensure we carefully consider every potential case of appendicitis,” which also avoids assigning fault while reinforcing vigilance [N4-R2][N4-R5].

Urgency should be expressed without sounding alarmist by using cautious but firm language that reflects the seriousness of the condition without creating undue fear. The evidence supports this balance because it highlights the importance of accurate assessment for each child, especially those in severe pain, and notes that missed appendicitis can have serious consequences [N1-F1][N4-R2]. A good phrasing is “especially those in severe pain” or “especially in children who are in severe pain,” which conveys urgency while remaining objective. It is also acceptable to say “we want to ensure we thoroughly evaluate every potential case of appendicitis, recognizing the importance of accurate assessment for each child” [N4-R2][N4-R5].

Phrasing that emphasizes teamwork and shared responsibility is consistent with the evidence on teamwork and shared decision-making. The evidence on teamwork in healthcare indicates that teamwork is central to safer health care delivery [N6-R1]. The evidence on shared decision-making also supports collaborative communication between providers and patients [N6-R3][N6-R4]. A professional team-oriented phrasing could be “we want to ensure we thoroughly evaluate every potential case of appendicitis, and we recognize that careful teamwork and shared responsibility are important for accurate assessment” [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Alternatively, “we want to ensure we thoroughly evaluate every potential case of appendicitis, because accurate assessment depends on careful teamwork and shared responsibility” is even more direct [N6-R1][N6-R3].

## 4) Final revised message

Based on the evidence and the grammar/tone review, here is a polished version of the patient’s final lines:

> Perform an initial exam focusing on right lower quadrant tenderness. Then calculate a pediatric appendicitis score to determine risk. If suspicion remains, obtain an ultrasound first. If ultrasound results are inconclusive, proceed with MRI. Consult pediatric surgery if imaging findings suggest appendicitis. We want to ensure we thoroughly evaluate every potential case of appendicitis, recognizing the importance of accurate assessment for each child, especially those in severe pain.

## 5) Why this works

This version preserves the core message while improving clarity, conciseness, and tone. It uses active voice and precise language (“calculate,” “obtain,” “proceed,” “consult”). It avoids vague or blaming phrasing. It also explicitly reflects the evidence-based triage pathway: clinical evaluation first, scoring as part of risk stratification, ultrasound-first imaging, MRI next when needed, and surgical consultation when imaging is suggestive [N1-F1][N2-F3][N3-F4]. The closing sentence reinforces the professional goal without sounding alarmist or too directive.

## 6) Additional note on the “everyone must do their best” alternative

If you still want a version that explicitly conveys shared responsibility without sounding negative, you could also say:

> We want to ensure we thoroughly evaluate every potential case of appendicitis, because accurate assessment depends on careful teamwork and shared responsibility, especially in children who are in severe pain.

This keeps the tone positive, emphasizes collaboration, and avoids placing the burden of “avoiding mistakes” on individuals [N4-R2][N6-R1][N6-R3].
